summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style biography and overview of Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the Persian polymath born c. 980 near Bukhara. It covers disputes over his madhab and family background, his birth and early education, and his philosophical distinction between essence and existence. It also describes his influence on medicine through the Canon of Medicine, his astronomical observations, his psychology and theology, and the honours named after him.
one_line: Biographical overview of Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the Persian polymath whose philosophy, medicine, astronomy and theology shaped Islamic and European thought.
key_facts: Avicenna was born c. 980 in Afšana, a village near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan.
Medieval historian Ẓahīr al-dīn al-Bayhaqī (d. 1169) considered Avicenna to be a follower of the Brethren of Purity.
Dimitri Gutas, along with Aisha Khan and Jules J. Janssens, demonstrated that Avicenna was a Sunni Hanafi.
Sharaf Khorasani believes Avicenna was an Ismaili, citing Avicenna's rejection of an invitation to the court of the Sunni Governor Sultan Mahmoud Ghazanavi.
According to Seyyed Hossein Nasr, the 14th century Shia faqih Nurullah Shushtari maintained that Avicenna was most likely a Twelver Shia.
According to his autobiography, Avicenna had memorised the entire Quran by the age of 10.
Avicenna distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud), arguing that the fact of existence cannot be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things.
Under the Samanids, Bukhara rivaled Baghdad as a cultural capital of the Islamic world.
George Sarton, author of The History of Science, described Ibn Sīnā as 'one of the greatest thinkers and medical scholars in history'.
Avicenna's Canon of Medicine linked Galen's medical writings with Aristotle's philosophical writings, significantly increasing his importance in medieval Europe.
From the early fourteenth to the mid-sixteenth centuries, Avicenna was ranked with Hippocrates and Galen as one of the acknowledged authorities, princeps medicorum ('prince of physicians').
Avicenna claimed to have observed Venus as a spot on the Sun, possibly during the transit of May 24, 1032; modern scholars suggest he may have mistaken a sunspot for Venus.
Avicenna argued that the stars are self-luminous, criticizing Aristotle's view that the stars receive their light from the Sun.
Avicenna's 'flying man' argument in The Cure I.1.7 defends the claim that the soul is without quantitative extension.
Avicenna's psychology is embodied in the Kitab al-nafs parts of the Kitab al-shifa (The Book of Healing) and Kitab al-najat (The Book of Deliverance), known in Latin as De Anima.
The Avicenna Mausoleum and Museum in Hamadan was built in 1952.
